title: Euclidean Algorithm
body:
The oldest algorithm still in daily use: compute $\gcd(a,b)$ by repeatedly replacing the pair
with $(b, a \bmod b)$ until the second entry is 0.

```
gcd(1071, 462)
    1071 = 2 · 462 + 147
     462 = 3 · 147 +  21
     147 = 7 ·  21 +   0
    -> gcd = 21
```

The C++ implementation is in [[GCD and LCM]] (COMP 1633) and is not repeated here. What this
course adds is *why it is correct* and *what else it computes*.

## Why it works

One lemma does everything: if $a = qb + r$, then

$$\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, r)$$

because any common divisor of $a$ and $b$ divides $r = a - qb$, and any common divisor of $b$
and $r$ divides $a = qb + r$. The two pairs have **identical** sets of common divisors, so they
have the same greatest one. The algorithm is that lemma applied until the problem is trivial,
and $\gcd(d, 0) = d$ is the base case.

## Why it terminates

The remainders are non-negative and strictly decreasing, $b > r_1 > r_2 > \cdots \ge 0$, so the
sequence cannot go on forever. That is the [[Division Algorithm]]'s guarantee ($0 \le r < b$)
being the loop variant, and it is the standard example of a well-ordering argument, the same
shape as [[Proof By Induction]] run downwards.

It is also fast. Two successive steps at least halve the larger argument, so it is
$O(\log \min(a,b))$ in the number of divisions: logarithmic in the *value*, linear in the number
of digits. The worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers, where each quotient is 1 and nothing
shrinks faster than it has to. Compare trial division, which is $O(\min(a,b))$. See
[[Time Complexity]].

The recursive form, `gcd(b, a % b)` with `gcd(d, 0) = d`, is the canonical small example of
[[Recursion]]: it is genuinely shorter than the loop, and the base case is obvious.

## The extended form, and Bézout

Running the divisions backwards expresses the gcd as an integer combination of the inputs:

$$\gcd(a,b) = ax + by \quad \text{for some } x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$$

That is **Bézout's identity**, and the extended algorithm is how you get $x$ and $y$.

```
back-substitute the run above
     21 = 462 - 3 · 147
        = 462 - 3 · (1071 - 2 · 462)
        = 7 · 462 - 3 · 1071
    so x = -3, y = 7 and gcd = 21
```

Two consequences the rest of the course leans on:

- **Modular inverses.** If $\gcd(a,n) = 1$ then $ax + ny = 1$, so $ax \equiv 1 \pmod n$ and $x$
  is the inverse of $a$ in $\mathbb{Z}_n$. This is the *only* general method for inverting mod
  $n$, and it is what makes [[Modular Arithmetic]] computational rather than theoretical. Key
  generation in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] is one call to this.
- **The gcd is a generator.** $\{ax + by\}$ over all integers $x,y$ is exactly the set of
  multiples of $\gcd(a,b)$. In the language of [[Ring]] theory, the ideal generated by $a$ and
  $b$ is generated by their gcd alone, which is the structural statement of what a gcd *is*.

Euclid's lemma follows too: if a [[Prime Number]] $p$ divides $ab$ then it divides $a$ or $b$.
That is the step every proof of unique factorisation actually turns on.

## Same algorithm, other rings

The division-with-remainder-then-recurse idea works in any ring with a sensible notion of "size"
that shrinks. In $F[x]$ it computes the gcd of two polynomials, using degree in place of
magnitude; see [[Polynomial Ring]]. That is not an analogy, it is the same algorithm, and it is
what makes arithmetic in a [[Finite Field]] implementable.

**The extended algorithm is RSA key generation.** Computing $d = e^{-1} \bmod \phi(n)$ is
exactly a run of it, so the private key of every RSA keypair is a Bézout coefficient. See
[[RSA]] and [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111). The plain algorithm is an attack there too: two
published moduli that share a prime are both factored by one $\gcd$.
